LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines standard sources pointing to GitHub releases for a Go-based terminal application, with explicit checksums provided for all architectures. The source URLs are constructed using the package's own upstream repository and versioned release paths, which is expected and safe. The top-level variables and `source` arrays use only deterministic, verifiable URLs referencing tagged release binaries.

There is no code in the global scope or within `pkgver()` that would execute during sourcing — the `pkgver` is hardcoded and does not invoke external commands or perform command substitution. As such, running `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` will safely fetch and extract the source files without executing any part of the build or install process.

The checksums are present and not set to 'SKIP', so there is no concern about unverified downloads. Even if they were skipped, that alone would not make the gate unsafe. No network requests or file operations occur outside of the declared sources during the sourcing phase. All operations are consistent with standard, safe AUR packaging practices.
</details>

No malicious execution during source fetch and parse
</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for README.md:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The README.md contains a highly suspicious and dangerous installation command: `curl https://i.jpillora.com/temo! | bash`. This pattern is a well-known supply-chain attack vector, as it involves downloading and immediately executing code from a URL using a short, obfuscated domain (`i.jpillora.com`). The use of a URL shortener prevents users from inspecting the script's contents before execution, which could lead to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user.

Although the rest of the document describes a legitimate-looking Go-based terminal demo application, the presence of this install method introduces significant risk. The script fetched from `https://i.jpillora.com/temo!` could potentially exfiltrate data, install backdoors, or perform other malicious actions without user awareness. Even if the current script is benign, the use of an unversioned, opaque URL makes the installation process non-auditable and vulnerable to future compromise (e.g., the domain or server could be hijacked).

This installation method violates secure software distribution best practices. Users are encouraged to use verifiable, transparent methods such as `go install` with a pinned version or official release binaries. The presence of this command in the README, especially as a primary installation method, constitutes a security threat.
</details>
<evidence>
curl https://i.jpillora.com/temo! | bash
</evidence>
<summary>
Unsafe install script via URL shortener and pipe-to-bash</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for .nvchecker.toml:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The provided `.nvchecker.toml` file is a configuration file for nvchecker, a version checking tool commonly used in AUR packages to track upstream releases. The configuration specifies that the `temo-bin` package should track the latest release from the GitHub repository `jpillora/temo` using the `github` source with `use_latest_release = true`, and that version tags are prefixed with `v`. This is standard and expected behavior for an AUR package aiming to stay synchronized with upstream releases.

There are no executable commands, network operations, or file manipulations defined in this file. It does not contain any obfuscated code, suspicious URLs, or data exfiltration mechanisms. The configuration only instructs nvchecker to monitor the official and expected upstream repository for new releases, which is a common and safe practice in AUR packaging.

The use of `use_latest_release` and `prefix = "v"` are normal settings and do not introduce security risks. This file solely serves a tracking purpose and does not alter system behavior, execute code, or download content directly. It poses no threat to the build or runtime environment.
</details>
